title: FROM DEATH TO LIFE
paragraphs: There are moments in every human story that feel like funerals.
Not the kind with flowers, caskets, and cemetery soil.
The secret sin that slowly hollowed out the soul.
The night someone sat on the edge of their bed staring into darkness wondering if God could still want someone like them.
Many people are still breathing while carrying entire graveyards inside them.
And Scripture begins with a startling truth:
Humanity's greatest problem was never merely suffering.
The Greek word Paul uses is νεκρός (nekros).
Paul does not describe humanity as wounded, struggling, or merely imperfect.
He describes us as spiritually dead.
That truth offends modern culture because we prefer the language of self-improvement.
Scripture speaks the language of resurrection.
A corpse does not educate itself back to life.
And that miracle has a name.
The story of redemption is not the story of good people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of dead people being raised.
Everything in the Gospel hinges upon this reality.
The Bible's opening pages reveal that humanity was created for life.
"Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life."
The Hebrew phrase is נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים (nishmat chayyim).
They were personally fashioned by God and animated by His breath.
Relationship with God was the environment in which humanity flourished.
The serpent's deception in Genesis 3 was not merely about eating forbidden fruit.
It was about replacing God's authority with human autonomy.
It was the declaration that humanity would define good and evil for itself.
The result was immediate spiritual death and eventual physical death.
The first response to sin was not confession.
And ever since, humanity has become remarkably skilled at hiding.
Behind carefully crafted images that convince others we are alive while our hearts quietly decay.
Yet Scripture refuses to flatter us.
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
The Greek word translated "fall short" is ὑστερέω (hystereō).
It carries the idea of lacking, failing to attain, coming behind.
Every human being has missed the mark.
Every person stands equally in need of grace.
This is where many stories would end.
But the Gospel is unlike any story ever written.
Because God did not walk away.
He moved toward the very people who ran from Him.
Even in Eden, judgment was accompanied by promise.
Genesis 3:15 contains what many theologians call the Protoevangelium—the first announcement of the Gospel.
A coming offspring would crush the serpent.
The story was still being written.
Throughout the Old Testament, shadows of resurrection began appearing everywhere.
Noah emerged from judgment into a new world.
Israel passed through the Red Sea from slavery into freedom.
Jonah emerged from the fish after three days.
Ezekiel saw a valley of dry bones rise again.
All of it whispered the same promise:
Not merely as a moral example.
In John 11, Jesus stood outside the tomb of Lazarus.
"I am the resurrection and the life."
Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή.
(Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.)
"I am the resurrection and the life."
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not merely claim to provide resurrection.
Life was standing in front of the grave.
Then came two words that shattered death's silence:
And a dead man walked out of his tomb.
But it was also a preview.
Because Lazarus would eventually die again.
Jesus was preparing the world for something greater.
The scandal of the cross cannot be overstated.
The Son of God was mocked.
The One who created life submitted Himself to death.
The Hebrew word for pierced is מְחֹלָל (mecholal), carrying the idea of being wounded, profaned, or fatally pierced.
The Messiah would suffer not for His own sin, but for ours.
At Calvary, every scandal of human rebellion collided with divine mercy.
This is the heart of substitutionary atonement.
Jesus took the place we deserved.
Paul summarizes it with breathtaking simplicity:
"He made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf."
The innocent died for the guilty.
The Holy One for the unholy.
The body of Jesus was placed inside a tomb.
For three days, it looked like death had won.
The Greek word used repeatedly throughout the New Testament is ἀνίστημι (anistēmi).
The resurrection is the foundation upon which Christianity stands.
Without it, there is no Gospel.
Because if Christ conquered death, then death is no longer the final authority.
Sin is no longer the final authority.
Failure is no longer the final authority.
Your worst chapter is not the final authority.
The resurrection means God specializes in impossible endings.
Many people assume salvation is merely about going to heaven someday.
But Scripture describes something far more radical.
A person united with Christ experiences resurrection life now.
The Greek phrase καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means a new creation of a different kind.
The Gospel does not merely improve lives.
This is why some of the most powerful testimonies in history begin with scandal.
Not because they became strong enough.
The enemy points to your past.
The enemy points to your failures.
The enemy says your life is over.
Jesus says, "Behold, I am making all things new."
Perhaps that is where you find yourself today.
Still carrying something that feels dead.
A faith that once burned brightly.
A heart exhausted from fighting battles nobody else can see.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly circumstance will immediately change.
But it does promise something even greater.
He walks into darkness and calls forth life.
What He did for Lazarus physically, He still does for sinners spiritually.
The same power that raised Christ from the dead is the power that transforms lives today.
Because Jesus Christ remains the Resurrection and the Life.
And this is the beautiful paradox at the center of Christianity:
The greatest scandal in history became the greatest demonstration of grace.
The tomb looked like the end.
The grave was real—but so was the voice that called life out of it.
